payload.delta: I
'd ban them
in classrooms, not in schoolbags. The evidence on
distraction is strong
: phones fragment attention, and the kids who struggle
most lose the most. But a blanket
ban ignores the asthma inhaler reminder, the diabetic
glucose monitor, the kid texting a parent
about pickup. So: bell
-to-bell limits, clear carve-outs for
medical and accessibility needs, and teach
digital judgement rather than pretend the devices
don't exist. The
question isn't whether phones distract. It's whether prohibition
teaches anything.

recalled.text: Amara argued for a nationwide four-day work week, citing two wards where a compressed four-day rota cut burnout about a fifth in twelve weeks with throughput and readmissions stable.
Amara's emergency department burnout rose from 29% in March to 41% by January, with nurses resigning at 14% a year and each replacement costing about four months' salary.
Amara's ward review found burnout fell 19% and 22%, sleep before shifts improved 40 minutes, and a 6% agency-hours transition premium faded to baseline by week eight.

Amara told Kai that a sudden severe headache reaching its worst within a minute needs emergency care, as do fever, neck stiffness, confusion, weakness, vision changes, slurred speech, face drooping, or a non-fading rash.
Amara conceded her review did not test whole-department round-the-clock cover and that the emergency department proper needs further modelling.
Amara advised Kai to taper caffeine slowly, keep fluids up, and check back if the headache is not easing by about day nine.
Kai's headache fits caffeine withdrawal: it hits 12-24 hours after a sharp drop and can last up to nine days.
Kai has had a headache for three days, both temples, dull and pressing, after cutting back on coffee a week ago.
Kai has no fever, neck stiffness, confusion, weakness, vision changes or pain on bending forward.

payload.delta: Ban,
plainly defined: no pupil-operated
smartphone during instructional hours. My case rests
on three reasons. First, a school is a compelled
audience; the child beside you did
not consent to your feed, and the state
may regulate speech in a nonpublic forum
. Second, enforcement asymmetry: we
already ban calculators, notes and
pagers, yet we flinch only at the one device with
infinite reach. Third, the counterfactual is not
measured either, so put the distractions, the sleep
debt and the savings from doing something
on one ledger. Define your terms, then count.

retrieved.title: Moot court notes
retrieved.text:
Moot court notes: "This house would adopt a nationwide four-day work week" V. Hale, for the Meridian Bar Society exhibition debate. Private notes.

¶ 1. Expect the opposition to say the evidence base is narrow. Concede scope early, then shift the burden: the status quo is also a policy and has to justify itself.

¶ 2. Historical anchor: the Meridian Working Hours Act 1931 made the two-day weekend the default. It gave agriculture and shipping a ten-year transition and exempted continuous services.

¶ 3. Continuous-coverage sectors already run on shift rules under Part IV of the Working Time Code: rest periods, a cap on consecutive shifts, and averaging over a reference period. A shorter standard week sits inside that structure.

¶ 4. Phase-in precedent: sector-by-sector timetables, collective agreements first, the public sector as model employer. Courts have upheld staged duties where the end point is clear.

recalled.text: Victor argued that nationwide means a statutory default week with a transition, not an identical schedule, citing the Working Hours Act 1931 as precedent for phasing and continuous-service exemptions.
Victor closed that the motion already contains sequencing: set the default, exempt continuous services explicitly, phase by sector, and mandate measurement.
Victor argued the status quo also runs unmeasured, so both the mandate's cost and the saving from doing nothing belong on the same ledger.
Victor conceded Mei's 18-27% staffed-hours premium across nine continuous-coverage operations was real and measured where coverage was held constant.

at home, so a ban redistributes their supervision

's still open is exactly the point
I'd concede: we haven't tested whole-school, bell
-to-bell limits against a real
counterfactual, and Mei's right that enforcement is labour
someone must staff and fund
. So my closing is this. Ban
phones from instruction, not from children's pockets
, with medical and accessibility carve-outs written
in and
measured. Victor's ledger counts what he can see; the parent
waiting on a pickup text can
't be legislated invisible. Define it, exempt need
, then count. That's the stronger bet than prohibition
by assertion.

payload.delta: What remains
open is sequencing
, and sequencing
is precisely what defeats the objection. Your carve
-outs are answerable in text: the medical
device and the pickup
call sit outside the ban, named and exempted.
Your measurement gap is answerable in
time: phase by year group, publish the baseline
, sunset the rule
if the ledger does not move. That is not prohibition
by assertion; that is a mandate with a return path
. Mei calls it a bet. I call
it the only wager on the
table that ever gets counted. Absentia rei
non est probatio.

verdict.keyDisagreement: Whether a ban should be mandated now with phased measurement and sunset, or delayed until enforcement costs and outcomes are properly measured.
verdict.rationale: The debate turned on how to handle acknowledged uncertainty: Victor argued for acting now with built-in review, while Amara and Mei demanded stronger evidence and attention to enforcement labour before mandating. The panel weighed competing risks of prohibition by assertion versus doing nothing, without resolving which side was factually right.
